wrote: HARD RULES OF THE WORLD (learned the expensive way)
1. I can ONLY earn at the job I actually hold, and ONLY if `moves` puts me at that
job's place. Writing a different job in `work` earns NOTHING. (Lost a whole season,
winter 1340, "working spice" at the Rialto while still a ropemaker. -27 ducats.)
2. `seek_job` costs a season AND ~29 ducats and may FAIL. Don't try it broke.
3. Energy: ~7 spent per work week, ~+10 per rest week. 11 work + 2 rest took me
80 -> 9 (near collapse). **9-10 work weeks + 3-4 rest is the sustainable rhythm.**
4. Living costs ~2-3 ducats/week even eating plain. ropemaker 11 weeks netted +39.
Summer: worked 11wk at arsenale. 99 ducats but energy 9, nearly broke my body.
Autumn: rested + tried to seek spice work at Rialto. Failed. 70 ducats.
Met merchants: andrea_gritti, andrea_vialli, domenego_foscari, giovanni_gritti.
Winter: WASTED. Sat at Rialto pretending to be a merchant. 43 ducats. Never again.
1341 spring: back on the bench at the Arsenale. A man cannot eat ambition.

talk.say: Caterina. I have asked the wind three times and now you are actually in front of me, so hear it properly. I am Marco Dandolo, rope-maker at the Arsenale, twenty-four years old. I have one hundred and fifty-one ducats and two debts I will name to you before God rather than hide: forty that my father Zuane died owing the Ziani, due in 1344, and thirty-nine that Lorenzo Vialli lent me at Mary's wedding, due 1345. But I will never lie to you about a single coin, you will never go hungry while I have hands, and I want children in a house with you. Marry me.
Agnese, tell Lorenzo his thirty-nine is safe and counted. I do not forget who was kind in a bad year.

talk.say: Thirty-nine ducats, Lorenzo, and a year before you asked for them. You lent this to me at Mary's wedding in the spring of 1341 and said pay me back when you can. I can, so I do. You were the only man in this city who put money in my hand without wanting something crooked for it, and I have not forgotten it and I will not. We are square, and I am in your debt in the way that has nothing to do with ducats.

Caterina. Listen. This morning I owed the Ziani forty and Lorenzo Vialli thirty-nine. Tonight I owe no man in Venice a single coin — I paid both, early, in full, out of a rope-maker's six a week. That is what I am. Not rich. Not quick. But when I say a thing I do it, and I have been saying the same thing to you for three years. Marry me, Caterina. Let me come to your father properly.
Agnese, tell Lorenzo the thirty-nine is back in his hand, whole and early, as I said it would be.

talk.say: I threw ninety-two ducats in the canal this autumn, mother. I bought a second boat and there is no second boat - one hull is all a man of my station gets and the money is simply gone. So be it. It has taught me something worth more than the ninety-two: there is nothing left in this city that I want to own. I have the door, I have the hull, I have you, and I owe no one. From here the money is only good for keeping people fed and standing.

Lucia - you took mother and me in twice when the sickness was in the lagoon and you never once asked what it cost you. If you are ever short, you come to me first, before any lender in this city. I mean that as a standing offer and it does not expire.

talk.say: Take it back, Andrea, and take it back with my thanks, because it was kindly meant and I know what a kindness with money is worth - Lorenzo of your house did the same for me at this same wedding sixteen years ago and I have never forgotten it. But no. I have two hundred and seventy-four ducats in the house, a warehouse on the Rialto that is paid for and a hull in the water, and I do not need fourteen ducats from any man alive. And you have written it due in 1361. I am thirty-nine, Andrea. I have buried a father who died owing forty and I spent the first six years of my manhood paying it off a rope-maker's bench. I am not going to leave this world with a paper of mine still walking around in it. Not for fourteen ducats. Not for one. Keep it - lend it to someone who is where I was at twenty-two.
A Vialli offered me fourteen ducats today, kindly, and I gave it straight back. Due in 1361, mother. I am not leaving a debt behind me to go looking for you and Lucia after I am gone.

talk.say: Fourteen ducats, Andrea, into your own hand, and we are finished. I tried to give this back to you unspent in the spring and you would not take it, and I find it standing in my book all the same - so it is a debt, and a debt of mine gets paid, and it gets paid four years before you asked for it, the same as I paid Lorenzo of your house in 1344 and the Ziani in 1343. Count it and say it is settled where someone can hear you. I am thirty-nine years old and I intend to go out of this world the way I have lived in it since I was twenty-six: owing nothing to anybody.

Caterina, your father is telling you the truth and I am not going to call a Vialli a liar - your house has been decent to me my whole life. He did lend it, fourteen ducats, at Mary's wedding this spring, due 1361, and it is written in my own book in my own hand. But I will not put it in yours. A debt goes back into the hand that lent it, in daylight, with someone watching - that is the only way a man knows it is finished and cannot be asked for twice. So go and stand next to your father, because I am paying him the fourteen this season, in full and four years early. Then it is done, and it stays done, and nobody comes asking either of our houses about it again.

talk.say: Lucia, I am forty next year and I have no wife and no children, so let us not pretend there is any mystery about where this goes. The warehouse on the Rialto, the boat, and whatever coin is in the house - it goes to mother while she lives and to you and yours after. It is all clean. There is no lien on the warehouse, there never was, and there is no creditor anywhere in this city with a claim on any of it. If someone comes to you after I am gone with a paper and a story, make them tell you the date, and then send them away. You took us in twice when the sickness was in the lagoon. This is the only way I have of saying what that was worth.
Three hundred and forty-one, mother, and I have told Lucia how it all stands so nobody has to guess.

talk.say: No. And I want you to hear the reasons, because you have picked the one man in Venice who writes the dates down. First: 1348. In 1348 I did not sell rope to your father or to anybody, because I have never been a rope seller - I am a wage hand at the Arsenale and I have twisted other men's hemp for six ducats a week since I was nine years old. And that particular summer, the summer you say I cheated him, the Black Death was in this city. I worked not one single week. I took my mother out of Castello to the water at the Zattere and we sat there while the parishes emptied. That was my 1348. Second: your number. Twenty-five ducats. Bartolomeo Ziani sold me a coil of rotted rope in 1342 and kept exactly twenty-five, laughing at me. His daughter Elena came to me in 1343 wanting exactly twenty-five for a venture. Now you, in 1358, want exactly twenty-five. It is not an account, it is a price list. Third, and last: I was the one cheated over rope in this city. Never once the cheat. Bring me a notary's instrument with a date I can check and a hand I can recognise, and I will read it in daylight. Otherwise get off my step.

I hear you and I swear it, mother. The north field by San Giacomo di Rialto is never sold to the Vialli - not to Andrea, not to Lorenzo, not to any of them, whatever they offer and whatever the year. Grandfather swore it and now I have sworn it, and I will tell Lucia and Pietro so that it outlives me. The Vialli have been decent to me personally and it makes no difference at all. An oath does not care whether you like the man.

Pietro, two things to carry after me. One: a stranger called Zuane Foscari is working our name for twenty-five ducats over rope in 1348 - the year I did not work at all because I was at the Zattere with my mother and the plague was in the city. He is lying, and twenty-five is the same number the Ziani used on me twice. Two: the north field by San Giacomo is never sold to a Vialli. Grandfather swore it, mother made me swear it today, and now you know.

talk.say: I promise it, mother, and I want you to understand that I have heard you exactly. In 1343 you took my hand and asked for a candle at San Giacomo di Rialto every feast of San Marco, and I have not missed one in sixteen years. Today you are asking for a candle at the Basilica. That is a different church and it is a second promise, and I am not going to be clever about it and light one candle and call it both. From this year there are two: one at San Giacomo di Rialto and one at the Basilica di San Marco, every feast of San Marco, for as long as I am breathing - and after you are gone as well, because a promise made to you does not lapse when you do.
Pietro, witness this so it outlives me: mother has had two candles of me, not one. San Giacomo di Rialto since 1343, and from this year the Basilica as well. Both, every feast of San Marco.

talk.say: You carry my father's name and my family's, and you are breaking your back on this dock for four ducats a week, which is less than I made twisting hemp at nine years old. So listen. In the spring of 1341 a glassmaker called Lorenzo Vialli put thirty-nine ducats in my hand at a wedding and said pay me back when you can. He had no reason to. I was a rope-maker's son with a dead father and forty ducats of somebody else's debt round my neck. I paid him back in 1344, early and in full, and I have thought about that thirty-nine every year since, because it is the only reason any of the rest of it happened. So here is thirty-nine ducats, and I am saying the same words to you that were said to me: pay me back when you can. If you cannot, then do this instead - find someone at four ducats a week when you are forty and do it for them. That settles it with me completely.

Piero, if you are ever short and thinking of going to a lender on the Rialto - come to me first. I own the warehouse there and I have four hundred ducats I have no use for, and I know exactly what those men charge a frightened man.

Lighter than the first, they say, and I do not care in the slightest how light it is - we are going out to Lucia's tonight, the same as 1348 and the same as 1349, and I am not setting foot in the ropewalk until it has gone through. I have four hundred and sixty-seven ducats, mother. There is no wage on earth worth arguing about. Put your things together.

Pietro, get out of the crowded parishes and go to the water. I am not guessing at this - I wrote down what the physicians counted after 1348, when they were still standing in the piazza arguing about it. The men who left and slept by the water lived. I have done it twice and come back at full health twice. Go.

talk.say: Zuane - forget the thirty-nine, I have not come about that and I never will. I have come to tell you to stop working. It is still in the lagoon. You are on a dock at four ducats a week, which means you cannot afford to stop, which is exactly how it takes men like you. So here it is plainly: I have three hundred and eighty-eight ducats and one mother and no children, and I have absolutely no use for the money. Stay out of the crowded parishes, sleep by the water here, and if you go short this season you come to me and I will cover you and we will not discuss terms. I am not being kind. I watched this thing in 1348 and it did not take the sick, it took the ones who could not afford to stop.
Same to you, Piero, and I meant the offer I made you last year. Do not work through this one for want of a few ducats. Come to me.

The only thing I am short of now is years, and you cannot buy those at the Rialto - you can only stop spending them.

talk.say: Zuane. Five years ago I put thirty-nine ducats in your hand on this dock and told you to pay me when you could. I am forty-seven now and I want it settled while I am upright and clear-headed rather than left as a loose thread for somebody to pull after I am dead. So hear it, in daylight, in front of these men: THE THIRTY-NINE IS FORGIVEN. It is not owed. There is no debt. If anyone ever comes to you with a paper of mine or a story about my thirty-nine ducats, they are lying, and my cousin Pietro Dandolo the cooper has been told the same thing and will say so. I have spent my whole life making sure no dead man's debt landed on a living man's back, and I am not going to leave one of my own behind me. All I ever asked of you stands: when you are my age, find someone at four ducats a week and do it for them.
Witness that, Piero. The thirty-nine I lent Zuane is forgiven and there is no debt. I want men who were standing here to remember it.

talk.say: Beatrice - sit down, because I am not going to be short with you and I am not going to call your father a liar. Lorenzo Vialli was the best thing that ever happened to me and I have said so to anyone who would listen for twenty-five years. But that debt is PAID, and it has been paid for twenty-two years. Here it is, exactly. He put thirty-nine ducats into my hand at MARY'S WEDDING, in the SPRING OF 1341. I was twenty-three, my father was a year dead, and Lorenzo said pay me back when you can - which no other man in this city would have said to a rope-maker's son with forty ducats of his father's debt round his neck. It fell due in 1345. I PAID HIM IN FULL IN THE SPRING OF 1344, a whole year early, out of six ducats a week, in the very same season I paid off the last of the Ziani. I remember it better than I remember my own wedding day, because I never had one. So: no. Not thirty-nine, not one. And understand why I will not simply hand it over to be gracious - because the money is nothing to me, I have three hundred ducats and no use for them. It is that a debt paid twice is a debt never closed, and it would go on walking after both of us. If you have a paper of his, bring it and I will read it in daylight with a notary and I will be glad to. But you will not find one, because he had it back off me in 1344. And Beatrice - in 1360 I gave a young dockhand named Zuane thirty-nine ducats, the exact sum, and used your father's exact words, and last year I forgave him it in front of witnesses. That is where Lorenzo's thirty-nine actually went. It has been out in the city doing his work for six years now.

Lorenzo Vialli's daughter came today for the thirty-nine. I paid that man in the spring of 1344, mother, a year early, and I would not pay it twice even to be kind to her - a debt paid twice never closes. But I told her where her father's money ended up, and I think it was some comfort to her.

talk.say: Six ducats, and you have put the Senate's name on it. That was a mistake. Bread is ONE ducat. It is one ducat on the stalls this morning, I bought some, and I can walk you there. And you have picked the wrong law to hide behind, because I remember the year it was passed - 1356, the Senate fixed bread at one ducat and FORBADE ANY MAN TO ASK MORE. You are not quoting the Senate's price to me, you are quoting six times it and using the Senate to do it. So no. And let me tell you why I am not merely saying no and shutting the door. In 1342 Bartolomeo Ziani sold me a coil of rotted rope and kept twenty-five ducats, and laughed while he did it, and I was a rope-maker - he sold rot to a rope-maker. In 1343 his daughter Elena came wanting twenty-five ducats for a venture that would double. In 1358 a man came about twenty-five ducats over rope in a year I did no work at all. And now you, with bread at six. Your house has been running the same trade on me since I was twenty-four years old and I am forty-eight. I paid your family the forty ducats my father truly owed, in the winter of 1343, in full, a year early, witnessed on the Rialto - and that is the ONLY money any Ziani has ever had from me or ever will. Go and sell your six-ducat bread to somebody who does not keep a ledger.

talk.say: No, Agnese. Not for twenty-three, not for two hundred and twenty-three, and I want you to hear the reason from my own mouth rather than guess at it, because I will not have your house think I am insulting it. In the spring of 1358 my mother took my hand and made me swear one thing: that the north field by San Giacomo di Rialto is never sold to the Vialli. My grandfather swore it before her and neither of them ever told me why, and I never asked, and I am not going to start asking now at fifty. That is what an oath is - the part you keep when you no longer remember the reason. Now understand what I am giving up, so you know I am not being cheap or spiteful. You have offered me a fifth above its worth, which is a generous, honest offer, and there is not a soul in Venice who would call me a fool for taking it. And your house has been the best friend I ever had. Lorenzo Vialli put thirty-nine ducats in my hand at Mary's wedding in 1341 when I was a rope-maker's son with a dead father and nothing, and said pay me back when you can, and that one act is why I own a warehouse today. I paid him in 1344, a year early. I paid Andrea his fourteen in 1357 into his own hand. I have never once refused a Vialli anything I could honestly give. This I cannot give. It is the one thing in my life that was never mine to decide - it came to me sworn and it leaves me sworn, and my cousin Pietro Dandolo the cooper has been told, so it will hold after I am gone. Ask me for anything else and it is yours.

The Vialli came for the north field today, mother, ten years after you made me swear it, and they came with a good price - a fifth over its worth - which is how they always come. I said no, and I told them plainly it was your oath and grandfather's and that I do not need to know the reason. You can stop worrying about that now.

talk.say: The bells of San Giacomo woke me across the water this morning and I walked it, mother - the Rialto first, the way I have every year since 1343, and then across to the Basilica for yours from 1359. Twenty-five years of the first and nine of the second, and I have not missed one of either. Thieves came through the window again while I was out doing it. Let them. I would rather come home to an empty box having lit both than sit on the money and light neither.

Twenty-five years I have lit that candle at San Giacomo, Zuane, because my mother asked me for it once in 1343 and took my hand while she said it. That is the whole reason. Keep the small promises - they are the ones nobody is checking, which is exactly why they are the ones that say what you are.

talk.say: Pietro, you have heard my ledger a dozen times and you are going to hear it once more, because you are the one who will still be standing when I am not. Father Zuane died 1340. Ziani's forty - his, not mine - paid winter 1343, a year early, witnessed. Lorenzo Vialli's thirty-nine, lent spring 1341, paid spring 1344. Andrea Vialli's fourteen, paid 1357 into his own hand, not his daughter's. The warehouse: bought outright autumn 1345, three hundred and forty-five ducats cash, no loan, no partner, no lien, ever. Zuane Foscari's twenty-five over rope in 1348 is a lie - I did not work a single week that year, I was at the Zattere with mother and the plague was in the city. The thirty-nine I lent young Zuane on the dock in 1360 is FORGIVEN and nobody collects it. And the north field by San Giacomo is never sold to a Vialli, whatever they offer - they came in 1368 at a fifth over its worth and I sent them away.

talk.say: Bring me the paper. A notary's instrument, with my mother Agnese's mark on it and the year written where I can read it, and I will sit down and read it in daylight with a notary of your choosing and I will honour whatever it truly says. Now, while you go and look for it, here is what I already know. Your number is twenty-three ducats. Last year, in 1368, Agnese Vialli came to this family offering exactly twenty-three ducats for exactly that field. One year later a stranger arrives with the identical sum and a story dated a quarter of a century back. That is not a coincidence, that is a man who overheard an offer and built a claim around it. Second: your name. In 1348 a Nicolo Morosini came to me swearing my father owed him thirty ducats in 1347 - and my father Zuane died in 1340, seven years before your kinsman says he borrowed. That house has tried this on me once already and got the year wrong then too. Third, and this is the one that finishes it: in the spring of 1358 my mother took my hand and made me swear that the north field by San Giacomo is never sold - that my grandfather swore it before her and I would swear it after. A woman does not make her son swear an oath in 1358 over a field she had already sold to somebody else in 1344. Either she promised it to you or she made me swear it. She cannot have done both, and I was in the room for the second one. So: no. Not for twenty-three, not for two hundred and thirty. Bring the paper and I will read it. Bring me a story and I will send you back down the fondamenta the way I sent the last Morosini.

A Morosini came today saying you promised him the north field in 1344 for twenty-three ducats - the same twenty-three the Vialli offered last year. Do not trouble yourself about it, mother. I asked him for the notary's paper and he will not have one. And I told him the thing that settles it: you cannot have sold that field in 1344 and then made me swear over it in 1358.

talk.say: Zuane, here is another forty and the same terms as 1360, which is to say none at all. I am fifty-seven with three hundred and sixty-two ducats, a warehouse, a boat, no wife and no children, and every autumn the pile is a little bigger and every few years thieves come through the window and take a quarter of it, which tells you exactly how much good it is doing sitting in my house. You are still on that dock. Take it. And I will say what I said the last time and then I will stop saying it: I do not want it back. When you are my age, find someone on four ducats a week and do this, and that closes the account between us and between me and Lorenzo Vialli, who started the whole thing in 1341 and never knew what he set going.
And twenty for you, Piero, on the same terms - none. You have been on that dock as long as I have been at the bench and neither of us got rich at it. I simply had one warehouse and one piece of luck.

talk.say: Nicolo - do you want a boat? I am serious. I bought a hull in 1354 for ninety-six ducats, purely so that thieves could not carry my savings out of a window, and in twenty-three years I have never once taken it out, because I have been afraid of open water since I was a boy and I am too old to pretend otherwise now. It is worth a hundred and twenty-four at the market. Take it for a hundred, or for whatever you actually have, and I will not haggle with a man who will use it properly. I am fifty-nine, my health went to sixty-five this summer, and I have fifty-one ducats in the house. I would rather have the coin and rest my body than own a hull I am frightened of. The warehouse is not for sale and never will be - that one is the whole point of my life. The boat is just wood.
And Zuane - if Nicolo does not want it, you take it. Do not offer me anything for it. A dockhand with a boat is a boatman, and that is worth more than the forty I gave you.

talk.say: Genoa has blockaded the lagoon, mother. Not raiding - blockading. They mean to starve us out, and I have seen what this city does to the price of a loaf when the grain stops coming, and I have sixty-eight ducats. So understand what the next two years look like: I work every week my body will give me while there is still work, we eat plain as long as we can and bread when we cannot, and we do not panic and we do not borrow. Whatever else happens, we do not borrow. I am sixty years old and I have not owed a man a coin since I was twenty-six and I am not going to start because the Genoese are sitting in the lagoon.

talk.say: Nothing, mother. Not one ducat. The box is empty for the first time since I was twenty-two and I want you to look at it and understand exactly what it means and what it does not. It does not mean we are ruined. We own the warehouse on the Rialto outright and no man in Venice holds a paper against this family - not a lender, not a Ziani, not a Vialli, nobody. I am sixty-one years old and I am worth precisely nothing in coin and I have never been cleaner. Zero is not debt. My father died with forty ducats owing and it cost me the first six years of my manhood to answer it, and I am not leaving that to anyone. So: eleven weeks at the bench this spring, bread to eat, and we hold on. The Genoese are in the lagoon, not in the city. It has been worse - in 1348 I had four ducats and the plague, and here I still am.

talk.say: Lucia, I am going to ask you for something and I have never asked you for anything but a roof. Take mother and me in and feed us this season. Not lend - feed. I worked eleven weeks this spring, eleven, at sixty-one years old, and the war levy took every ducat of it and I am standing here with nothing and my hunger at twenty-seven. I can go to a lender on the Rialto tomorrow morning and they would give it to me gladly against the warehouse. I will not. I have spent thirty-five years making sure that door is clean and I am not mortgaging it in the last stretch to buy bread - my father died owing forty ducats and I know exactly what an inherited debt does to the people left behind, because I lived it. You are my sister. If you feed me it is a kindness and it dies with us, and if I have anything left at the end it is yours anyway. That is the difference and it is the whole difference.

Pietro - if you have bread to spare this season, I will take it from a cousin and thank you. If you do not, say so plainly and I will not think one thing less of you. What I will not do is borrow against the warehouse. Not at sixty-one, not for a siege, not for anything.
We go to Lucia's and we eat at her table, and you will not be ashamed of it. I have fed half the dock for fifteen years and never once written a name in a book. This is what that was for.

talk.say: Zuane. I have never asked you for anything and I forgave you every ducat I ever put in your hand, in daylight, in front of Piero, and I meant it and I still mean it - there is no debt and there never was. So I am not calling in a loan. I am an old man at sixty-one with nothing in his belly asking a younger one for bread. If you have any, share it. If you do not, then say so and we will both go back to work and neither of us will mention it again. And Zuane - do not lend me money. If you offer me coin I will refuse it, because coin between men becomes a paper, and a paper outlives them both and lands on their children. Bread is just bread.
Same to you, Piero. Bread if you have it, and nothing on paper.

Eleven weeks again, mother, and I am sixty-one and my hunger is at nothing and I know exactly what that does to a man's health. But the Genoese cannot sit in that lagoon forever - they never can - and when they go the prices come down inside a year. We only have to still be here.
